cases.name: a redirection target is a write
cases.why: The word after `>` is a write target.

cases.name: an append is a write
cases.why: The word after `>>` is a write target.

cases.name: a command with no write has no target
cases.why: A command that only reads names no target.

cases.name: an input redirection is not a write
cases.why: The word after `<` is read.

cases.name: a here-string is not a write
cases.why: The word after `<<<` is data.

input.command: git commit -m "a; rm x" && touch web/a.ts

cases.name: quoted separators do not split a command
cases.why: A `;` inside quotes belongs to the word.

cases.name: a line feed splits a command
cases.why: A line feed starts the next command.

cases.name: fd duplication and closing are not targets
cases.why: `2>&1` and `2>&-` name a descriptor.

input.command:
cat > notes.md <<'EOF'
rm src/core/a.ts
mkdir build
> quoted line
EOF

cases.name: a heredoc with a quoted delimiter has a body that is data
cases.why: No line of the body is a command.

cases.name: a heredoc with an unquoted delimiter has a body that is data
cases.why: No line of the body is a command.

input.command:
cat > web/setup.sh <<'EOF'
mkdir -p build
rm -rf dist
EOF
touch web/after.txt

cases.name: a command after a heredoc is read
cases.why: The body ends at the delimiter line.

input.command:
cat <<-EOF > a.txt
	rm x
	EOF
rm b

cases.name: <<- strips the tabs of the delimiter line
cases.why: With `<<-` the delimiter line may start with tabs.

input.command:
cat <<EOF > a.txt
rm x
	EOF
EOF
rm b

cases.name: << does not strip the tabs of the delimiter line
cases.why: With `<<` a delimiter line that starts with a tab is part of the body.

input.command:
cat <<A >a.txt; cat <<"B" >b.txt
rm x
A
rm y
B
rm z

cases.name: two heredocs on one line have their bodies in order
cases.why: Each body ends at its own delimiter.

input.command:
cat <<EOF
rm x
EOF
rm y

cases.name: a heredoc body with carriage returns ends at its delimiter
cases.why: A carriage return before the line feed is not part of the delimiter.

cases.name: sed -i writes its file operand and not its script
cases.why: The first operand of `sed -i` with no `-e` is the script.

cases.name: sed -i with a backup suffix writes every file operand
cases.why: `-i.bak` is in-place with a suffix.

cases.name: sed -i with -e writes every operand
cases.why: With `-e` the operands are all files.

cases.name: sed -i with -f writes every operand
cases.why: With `-f` the operands are all files.

cases.name: sed with no -i writes nothing
cases.why: Without `-i` the operands are read.

cases.name: an awk program is not a path
cases.why: Awk writes nothing unless it redirects.

cases.name: cp writes its destination
cases.why: The last operand of `cp` is the destination.

cases.name: cp with many sources writes the last operand
cases.why: The last operand of `cp` is the destination.

cases.name: mv writes its destination
cases.why: The last operand of `mv` is the destination.

cases.name: ln writes its destination
cases.why: The last operand of `ln` is the destination.

cases.name: cp -t names the destination directory
cases.why: `-t` gives the destination before the sources.

cases.name: install writes its destination and skips the mode
cases.why: `-m` takes a value that is not a path.

cases.name: install -d writes every operand
cases.why: `-d` makes directories.

cases.name: cp with one operand has no target
cases.why: The gate does not guess a target.

input.command: echo hi > src/core/a.ts && rm web/old.ts; touch -d yesterday web/n.ts

cases.name: several commands each name their targets
cases.why: Redirections and commands on one line all count.

cases.name: truncate writes its file
cases.why: `-s` takes a value that is not a path.

cases.name: tee writes its operands
cases.why: Every operand of `tee` is a file.

cases.name: a target with a variable is left out
cases.why: A word that the shell decides at run time cannot be judged.

cases.name: a target with a command substitution is left out
cases.why: A word that the shell decides at run time cannot be judged.

cases.name: a program named by its path is read by its last segment
cases.why: `/bin/rm` is `rm`.

cases.name: the same target twice is listed once
cases.why: The list has no repeats.

cases.name: a flag that takes a value skips the value
cases.why: `touch -d` takes a date.

cases.name: an option terminator makes the rest operands
cases.why: After `--` a word that starts with `-` is a path.

cases.name: mkdir skips the mode
cases.why: `-m` takes a value that is not a path.

cases.name: a quoted target is read without its quotes
cases.why: Quotes and escapes are removed from a word.

cases.name: an escaped space joins a word
cases.why: A backslash before a space keeps the word together.

cases.name: a pipe starts a new command
cases.why: The command after `|` has its own targets.

cases.name: a background marker starts a new command
cases.why: The command after `&` has its own targets.

cases.name: a redirection that has no target ends the line
cases.why: A redirection operator at the end names no path.

cases.name: an unclosed quote runs to the end of the line
cases.why: The word holds the rest of the line.

description: The paths that a shell command writes, read from the command text.
